summary:
Russia presents severe and escalating legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the same legislation deems marriages null where a trans person marries someone of their same birth sex, and people with gender dysphoria are deprived of the right to adopt children.

The Supreme Court designated the non-existent "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols, spanning administrative and criminal codes, and has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. Since the designation, arrests have occurred for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours, and between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations, including the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

The expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression promoting "non-traditional" sexual relationships or making minors interested in gender transition. The 2013 statute targeted minors and was expanded in December 2022 to all age groups, also prohibiting materials giving minors a "desire to change their sex." Cases under these statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade; in 2023 alone there were more than 180 enforcement cases, exceeding all cases from 2013 to 2022 combined, with fines around 26 million rubles, and fines brought over 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over two years.

Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Enforcement has been swift and violent. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, with at least two other venues raided the same night. In December 2024 a Russian man arrested on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, and activists report the community living in fear, pushed into silence, flight and self-censorship.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented: in summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a Siberian conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only when police responded to a phone she found.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and does not designate hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity as such; such motivation is not an aggravating factor in sentencing, and the government does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are permitted. A July 2020 constitutional amendment banned same-sex marriage, and the 2021 ECtHR case Fedotova and Others v. Russia found Russia's refusal to recognise same-sex relationships a human rights violation; Russia left the court in 2022. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions.

Public opinion is markedly hostile: a 2022 survey found 74% of Russians said homosexuality should not be accepted, up from 60% in 2002, and a September 2021 survey showed support for equal rights for gays and lesbians at 33%. Moscow authorities have never approved a gay pride rally request, and in 2010 Russia was fined by the ECtHR for systematically refusing pride permits.

For those considering asylum, the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
The post-designation crackdown has driven mass emigration; foreign policy analysis describes the extremism designation fuelling a purge and exile of LGBT Russians, and reporting indicates emigration has become the only means of survival for many transgender Russians since the 2023 ban.

Regional variation exists within Russia: the autonomous republic of Chechnya is singled out in UK Home Office guidance as a particular social group context, implying heightened risk there relative to the national baseline.

The enforcement regime generates substantial state revenue, with propaganda-law fines exceeding 60 million rubles in two years, indicating institutional incentive to continue prosecutions.

outOfScopeNotes:
The exact scope of what constitutes "justifying" gender transition under the expanded propaganda law, and whether verbal or private expression carries the same penalty as public display, is not resolved in the source inventory.

Whether the 101 extremism convictions documented by Human Rights Watch include charges against foreign nationals, and the specific penalty ranges applied in each, is not sourced here.

The current operational status of consular services for trans travellers, and whether document gender markers affect visa issuance, is not addressed in the inventory.

Enforcement intensity outside major cities such as Moscow and St Petersburg is not well documented in these sources; the reported raids and arrests concentrate on urban venues.
